analogy.p: Imagine a never-ending roll of wallpaper with a repeating pattern of tulips. You make a second copy of the roll, slide it along by exactly one pattern repeat, and lay it over the first. Every tulip lines up with a tulip, so if you cut away the overlap, everything infinite cancels and you are left with just one finite strip: the length of one pattern. Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 is the sliding, and subtracting is the cutting away, and the finite strip is the whole number on the right-hand side of the equation. The analogy breaks down because with wallpaper you slide by any amount you like, whereas in maths you must slide by exactly one whole repeating block (or the tails will not match), and with a non-repeating start you need two copies slid by different amounts.
analogy.t: The photocopier and the carbon-copy trick

bullets: **Convert** a recurring decimal such as 0.7̇ or 0.2̇7̇ into a fraction in its simplest form.
**Prove** (show) that a recurring decimal is equal to a stated fraction, for example 0.2̇7̇ = 3/11.
Handle recurring decimals with a **non-repeating part** first, such as 0.1̇6 or 0.4̇1.
Handle recurring decimals with a **whole number part**, such as 2.1̇4̇.
Know that **every recurring and terminating decimal is a rational number**, so it can be written as a fraction of two integers.
Know how to tell, without dividing, whether a fraction will **terminate or recur**.
Use dot notation correctly: the dot goes over the **first and last digit** of the repeating block.
Command words you will see: **convert, show that, prove, write as a fraction in its simplest form**.
core.p: This point of the Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics Higher specification (Number) asks you to change a recurring decimal into a fraction, and to prove that a given recurring decimal equals a given fraction. It builds on converting fractions to decimals by division and sits alongside the idea of rational and irrational numbers. At Higher tier you must be able to do this algebraically, showing every line, because the question is usually worded 'Show that' or 'Prove that' and the method is what earns the marks, not the final answer, which is often given to you.

bullets: 0.7̇ means 0.7777777... (the 7 repeats forever).
0.2̇7̇ means 0.27272727... (the block 27 repeats).
A three-digit block: 0.142142142... is written 0.1̇42̇ with dots on the 1 and the 2, and the 4 in between repeats too.
0.16̇ means 0.16666... (only the 6 repeats; the 1 does not), which is different from 0.1̇6̇ = 0.161616...
The **repeating block** (the period) can be 1 digit long or many digits long: 1/7 = 0.142857 repeating has a block of 6 digits.
A recurring decimal never ends and never settles into zeros, which is why we cannot simply read off a fraction from the digits.
Words to use: **recurring**, **repeating**, **infinite**, **non-terminating**. A **terminating** decimal ends, for example 0.375.
On a calculator the display is rounded, so 0.666666667 shown on screen is really 0.6̇; always judge repetition from the exact pattern, not the rounded display.
core.p: A recurring decimal is a decimal whose digits repeat forever in a fixed pattern. We never write the repeating digits out forever; instead we use dots. A single dot over one digit means that digit repeats on its own. If a block of several digits repeats, a dot is placed over the first digit and over the last digit of the block, and everything between them also repeats. If you write the notation wrongly in the exam you can lose the accuracy mark, so learn it carefully.

bullets: **Rational number**: can be written as a/b where a and b are integers and b is not 0. Terminating and recurring decimals are all rational.
**Irrational number**: cannot be written as a fraction; its decimal never ends and never repeats. Examples: pi, the square root of 2, the square root of 3.
In a long division by b, only b possible remainders exist, so the decimal for a/b must repeat within b-1 digits at most (or terminate).
1/7 has the maximum possible block length of 6 digits (0.142857 repeating), because the remainders 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 all occur before 1 returns.
The algebraic method works because multiplying a recurring decimal by a power of 10 shifts the digits but leaves the same infinite tail, so subtraction removes the infinity.
Link to **surds and irrational numbers**: a question may ask you to decide whether a number is rational or irrational, so being able to convert recurring decimals matters.
Link to **proof**: 'show that' questions are small proofs, each line must follow logically from the previous.
core.h: Why recurring decimals can be written as fractions
core.p: A fraction a/b is what you get when you divide the integer a by the integer b. When you do long division the remainders can only be the numbers 0 to b-1, so after at most b steps a remainder must repeat, and from then on the digits repeat as well. That is why every fraction gives a terminating or a recurring decimal. The reverse is also true: every recurring decimal comes from some fraction, and the algebraic method finds it. A number that can be written as a fraction of two integers (with the denominator not zero) is called a rational number.

bullets: Step 1: write **let x = 0.7777...** (write several digits to show the pattern).
Step 2: multiply both sides by 10: **10x = 7.7777...**
Step 3: subtract the first equation from the second: **10x - x = 7.7777... - 0.7777...**, so **9x = 7**.
Step 4: divide by 9: **x = 7/9**.
Step 5: simplify if possible and, if asked, check on a calculator: 7 divided by 9 = 0.777...
Always subtract the **smaller from the larger** so that you get a positive number on the right-hand side.
Always show the lines '10x = ...' and the subtraction; marks are for the method (usually M1 for two correct lines with matching tails, M1 for subtracting, A1 for the fraction).
Example: 0.4̇ = 4/9; 0.1̇ = 1/9; 0.8̇ = 8/9. Pattern: a single repeating digit d gives **d/9**.
core.h: The core algebraic method (one repeating digit)
core.p: The standard method is to call the recurring decimal x, multiply it by a power of 10 so that the recurring part moves one full block to the left, and then subtract the original equation. Because the infinite string of repeating digits is exactly the same in both equations, it cancels, leaving a whole number (or terminating decimal) equal to a multiple of x. Divide to find x. For a single repeating digit we multiply by 10 because moving the decimal point one place right shifts one repeat.

bullets: Subtract: **100x - x = 27**, so **99x = 27**, so x = 27/99 = **3/11** after dividing top and bottom by 9.
For a three-digit block use **1000x - x = 999x**; for example 0.1̇42̇ = 142/999.
General pattern: a block of n repeating digits gives the block number over a denominator made of n nines: 0.3̇6̇ = 36/99 = 4/11; 0.0̇5̇ = 5/99.
Leading zeros inside the block count as digits: 0.0̇5̇ has a block of two digits (05), so multiply by 100, getting 99x = 5.
Always **simplify** the answer: 27/99 is not in simplest form until you divide by the highest common factor 9.
Common denominators that appear: 9, 99, 999. Knowing 99 = 9 x 11 and 999 = 27 x 37 helps you simplify quickly.
Check by dividing: 3 divided by 11 = 0.272727... confirms the answer.
core.p: If a block of n digits repeats, multiply by 10 to the power n (100 for two digits, 1000 for three digits, and so on). The reason is that you need to move the decimal point past exactly one complete block so the digits that follow the point in the new equation match the original equation exactly. If you multiply by the wrong power the tails do not line up and the subtraction will not cancel the infinite part, so the answer will not be a whole number.

bullets: For x = 0.16666...: **10x = 1.6666...** (point now just before the repeating 6) and **100x = 16.6666...** (one repeat further).
Rule of thumb: number of multiplications = digits before the repeat to place the point at the block, then the block length more.

Alternative shortcut for exams that allow it: split the decimal into a terminating part and a pure recurring part, for example 0.1666... = 0.1 + 0.0666... but the algebraic method is safer for full marks.
Check the result: 1 divided by 6 = 0.1666... ✓. 37 divided by 90 = 0.41111... ✓.
The denominator of such answers includes a factor of 10 (for example 90 = 9 x 10), because of the non-repeating digit.
Warning: do NOT subtract x from 10x here; that would leave the tail .6666... on the right and you cannot solve for x.
core.h: Recurring decimals with a non-repeating part
core.p: Sometimes some digits come after the decimal point before the repeating starts, as in 0.1666... or 0.4111.... The aim is the same: create two multiples of x whose repeating tails are identical. First multiply by a power of 10 to bring the decimal point to the start of the repeating block, then multiply by another power of 10 to move one full block further. Subtracting those two lines cancels the tails. This is the most common source of lost marks, because students try to use only x and 10x, whose tails are not matched.

bullets: Subtract: **100x - x = 212**, so **99x = 212**, so x = **212/99** (this is 2 14/99 as a mixed number).
Check: 212 divided by 99 = 2.141414... ✓.
The whole number part never affects the choice of multiplier; only the repeating block does.
For answers like 0.9̇: x = 0.999..., 10x = 9.999..., 9x = 9, so **x = 1**. This proves that 0.9̇ is exactly equal to 1, a favourite exam proof.
Negative recurring decimals: convert the positive version, then put the minus sign in front.
Always read whether the question wants an **improper fraction** or a **mixed number**.
core.h: Recurring decimals with a whole-number part
core.p: If the recurring decimal is greater than 1, such as 2.1414..., you can either convert only the decimal part and then add the whole number back on afterwards, or you can include the whole number in the algebra from the beginning. Both methods are acceptable. Including the whole number from the start is efficient because the final line gives an improper fraction, and you can then convert it to a mixed number if the question asks for one.

bullets: **Terminating**: simplest-form denominator has only prime factors 2 and/or 5, for example 3/8 (8 = 2x2x2), 7/20 (20 = 2x2x5), 9/125.
**Recurring**: any other prime factor remains, for example 5/6 (6 = 2x3), 2/7, 4/15 (15 = 3x5), 7/30.
**Simplify first**: 6/15 = 2/5 terminates, even though 15 contains a 3. Skipping simplification gives the wrong answer.
Typical question: 'Without a calculator, explain why 7/30 gives a recurring decimal.' Answer: simplest form, 30 = 2 x 3 x 5 includes a factor 3 which is not 2 or 5.
Typical question: 'Which of these fractions give terminating decimals?' Test each denominator in simplest form.
Link to **fractions and place value**: each decimal place is a power of ten, so terminating decimals are fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000 and so on.
core.h: Deciding whether a fraction terminates or recurs
core.p: You can predict the type of decimal without dividing. First write the fraction in its simplest form. Then factorise the denominator into primes. Our number system is base ten and 10 = 2 x 5, so a fraction only terminates if its denominator divides into some power of 10, which means its only prime factors are 2 and 5. If any other prime factor, such as 3, 7 or 11, is present in the simplified denominator, the decimal must recur.

bullets: 0.35 = 35/100 = **7/20** (divide top and bottom by 5).
For a decimal with n decimal places the denominator is 10 to the power n.
Compare with recurring: 0.35 = 35/100 but 0.3̇5̇ = 35/99. Same digits, different denominators.
This helps you remember: terminating uses 10, 100, 1000; recurring uses 9, 99, 999 (and combinations with 10).
When a question mixes both, convert each part separately then combine, for example 0.3̇ + 0.25 = 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12.
core.h: Terminating decimals to fractions (the easy direction)
core.p: For terminating decimals no algebra is needed. Write the digits over the correct power of 10 according to the last decimal place and then simplify. This is a useful check on your understanding, because the recurring method is simply the same idea but with the nine-based denominators needed to cope with the infinite repeat.

bullets: 0.3̇ + 0.6̇ = 1/3 + 2/3 = **1**, which is neat evidence that 0.9̇ = 1.
To compare sizes, convert to fractions with a common denominator, or compare enough decimal places carefully: 0.7̇ = 0.7777... is bigger than 0.77.
Never round before adding if the question asks for an exact answer; keep the fractions.
Use a **calculator check**: divide the numerator by the denominator and see that the repeating pattern matches the original decimal.
Ratio and probability questions sometimes give a recurring percentage such as 33.3̇%, which is exactly 1/3.
Interpret: 16.6̇% of an amount is 1/6 of the amount, a quick exact method.
core.p: Sometimes you are asked to work with the fractions you have found, for example to add or multiply two recurring decimals exactly. Converting to fractions gives an exact answer where the decimals would be only approximate. The ability to move between forms is exactly the kind of fluency that Edexcel's problem-solving objectives assess. It is also a good way to check answers.

bullets: Start with **'Let x = 0.2727...'** (not just 'x = 0.27').
Write the multiplied line directly beneath with the decimal points aligned: **100x = 27.2727...**
Write the subtraction as an equation: **100x - x = 27.2727... - 0.2727... = 27**, then **99x = 27**.
Finish: **x = 27/99 = 3/11**, simplifying and matching exactly what you were asked to show.
If the answer is given and you cannot reproduce it, check which power of 10 you used and whether you simplified.
Do not write '0.2727... = 27/99' as your only line; there must be algebra.
If the question says 'Prove', use a short concluding sentence such as 'Therefore 0.2̇7̇ = 3/11'.
Typical mark scheme: M1 for 100x = 27.2727...; M1 for subtracting; A1 for 99x = 27 or equivalent; C1 for the conclusion.
core.h: Presenting a full-mark 'show that' or 'prove' answer
core.p: A proof question gives you the answer, so every mark is for the method and the communication. Write the equations on separate lines, label them if it helps, say what you are doing, show the subtraction clearly, and end with the stated result. Examiners need to see that the infinite tails cancel, so write enough repeating digits (at least three or four) to make the pattern clear.

bullets: **Number**: rational versus irrational numbers; a rational number is any recurring or terminating decimal.
**Algebra**: solving linear equations and forming and manipulating expressions.
**Fractions**: simplifying with the highest common factor, converting between improper and mixed forms.
**Proof**: use algebra to prove statements, e.g. that 0.9̇ = 1 or that 0.4̇5̇ = 5/11.
**Surds**: irrational numbers such as the square root of 2 have non-repeating infinite decimals, so cannot be converted this way.
**Percentages**: recurring percentages such as 16.6̇% are exact fractions.
**Exam strategy**: calculator questions can verify your fraction by division; non-calculator questions need the algebra.
**Higher extension**: recognising that a/b with denominator containing a factor 3, 7, 11, 13 and so on must recur, and explaining the length of the repeating block is at most b - 1.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Recurring decimals connect to several other areas. In algebra, the method is linear equation solving; in number, it is part of the rational and irrational numbers family; in proof, it is a model of formal reasoning. At the very top of the Higher tier, you may need to combine recurring decimals with surds, indices or algebraic fractions, so being fluent here pays off.

exam: 'Show that' / 'Prove' recurring decimal questions are usually 2 or 3 marks (sometimes 4 for non-repeating start): M1 for the multiplied line, M1 for subtracting, A1 for the fraction or the conclusion.
Write the equations one under the other with decimal points aligned; examiners award marks for clearly seeing the tails cancel.
Write at least four digits of the pattern: 0.272727... not 0.27...
Use the phrase 'Let x = ...' to define your variable.
Check the answer by dividing the numerator by the denominator on a calculator, and say so; it costs 5 seconds.
For 'explain why 7/30 gives a recurring decimal' (2 marks): state the denominator in simplest form, factorise (2 x 3 x 5), then say the factor 3 means it cannot be a power of 10.
1-mark recall questions: 'Write 0.3̇ as a fraction' (1/3); learn 1/3, 2/3, 1/6, 1/9, 1/11 as decimals and fractions.
Do not round recurring decimals when asked for an exact fraction; rounding loses the accuracy mark.
If the question says 'give your answer in its simplest form', an unsimplified correct fraction typically scores A0.
Time: around 1 mark per minute, so a 3-mark proof should take about 3 minutes.

mistakes.r: Multiply by 100 for a two-digit block so the tails line up, giving 99x = 27.
mistakes.w: Using 10x - x for 0.2727... (multiplying by 10 when two digits repeat)

mistakes.r: Divide top and bottom by the HCF 9 to give 3/11; an unsimplified answer often loses the final mark.
Create two lines with identical tails: 100x - 10x gives 90x = 15, so 1/6.
Dots go over the first and last digits of the repeating block only; 0.142̇2̇... must be checked against the actual pattern.
mistakes.w: Placing dots incorrectly, e.g. 0.1̇42̇ when only 42 repeats

mistakes.r: Simplify first: 6/15 = 2/5, whose denominator has only the factor 5, so it terminates.
mistakes.w: Saying a fraction like 6/15 recurs because 15 has a factor 3

mistakes.r: Write at least three repeats such as 0.272727... so the pattern is clear.
mistakes.w: Writing only 0.27 as the first line (not enough digits)

mistakes.r: The proof shows 9x = 9 so x = 1 exactly; 0.999... is not 'just less than 1'.
mistakes.w: Giving the decimal 0.9 rather than saying 0.9̇ = 1

summary: You must convert recurring decimals into fractions (and prove given conversions) using algebra, deal with non-repeating starts and whole-number parts, and decide whether a fraction terminates or recurs. It matters because it links number, algebra and proof and appears as a 'show that' question worth 2 to 4 marks on Higher papers.

terms.d: A decimal in which a digit or a group of digits repeats forever in the same pattern.
A decimal that ends after a finite number of decimal places.
A number that can be written as a fraction a/b where a and b are integers and b is not zero.
A number that cannot be written as a fraction; its decimal neither terminates nor recurs.
The digit or digits that repeat; the dots go over its first and last digits.
A dot above a single repeating digit, or above the first and last digit of a repeating block.
A positive or negative whole number, or zero.
The top number of a fraction.
The bottom number of a fraction, showing how many equal parts make a whole.
A fraction in which the numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1.
The largest number that divides exactly into two or more numbers.
A factor of a number that is itself a prime number.
Fractions with the same value, such as 27/99 and 3/11.
A logical argument, with each step following from the last, that shows a statement is always true.

worked.q: Write 0.4111... = 0.41̇ as a fraction in its simplest form. [3 marks]
steps: Multiply by 10 to place the point before the repeating 1: 10x = 4.1111...
x = 37/90. Is it in simplest form? 37 is prime and does not divide 90, so yes.

worked.q: Convert 2.1̇4̇ to a mixed number and (b) explain why 5/12 gives a recurring decimal. [3 + 2 marks]
steps: (b) 5/12 is in simplest form (5 and 12 share no factor).
12 = 2 x 2 x 3 contains the prime factor 3, which is neither 2 nor 5, so 5/12 cannot be a fraction over a power of 10 and gives a recurring decimal (0.416̇).
